title: Distribution, Labor Mechanics & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In a people business, revenue is vanity, gross margin is sanity, and billing your customer before payroll clears on Friday is survival.
epigraph.author: Services Operator's Rule

web_blocks.html: ABM Industries wins business through an enterprise Request for Proposal (RFP) process [7, 18]. Commercial landlords, airlines, school districts, and manufacturers issue competitive multi-year tenders [7, 18]. Contract terms typically span 3 to 5 years [18]. Evaluation criteria prioritize verified safety records, union labor compliance, and technical credentials [7, 18]. Pricing models evaluate cost per square foot or hourly labor billing rates [18]. Once onboarded, ABM expands client wallet share by bundling specialized facility services [10, 18]. Account managers add stationary engineering, parking operations, or RavenVolt microgrids to legacy janitorial contracts [10, 18]. Teams also capture high-margin variable 'tag work' outside baseline service agreements [18].

The primary unit-economic risk centers on contract structure and hourly labor mechanics [7, 18]. A substantial share of ABM's 113,000 employees work under union collective bargaining agreements [2, 7]. These arrangements involve multiemployer pension funds and health welfare plans [2, 7]. Under cost-plus contracts, wage increases, payroll taxes, and benefit expenses pass directly to clients [18]. ABM collects an agreed management markup fee on top of these allowable costs [18]. Under fixed-price contracts, ABM absorbs mid-contract wage inflation [7, 18]. These fixed-price terms predominate across commercial office and education accounts [7, 18]. Management must invoke economic adjustment clauses or optimize staffing schedules to protect margins [7, 18].

web_blocks.html: This cash waterfall highlights working-capital volatility and the ELEVATE ERP transformation [25, 26]. CEO Scott Salmirs launched the ELEVATE program in December 2021 [25]. The initiative undertook an enterprise-wide overhaul of legacy financial, billing, and workforce systems [25, 26]. Management aimed to unify disparate systems following the GCA and Able Services acquisitions [25, 26]. However, the initial rollout triggered significant operational friction [26, 27]. Billing delays elevated unbilled contract receivables across regional operating branches [26, 27]. Consequently, operating cash flow dropped to $20.4 million in FY2022 [24, 27]. Cash flow subsequently stabilized at $243.3 million in FY2023 [24, 27]. Operating cash flow reached $226.7 million in FY2024 and $234.4 million in FY2025 [24, 27]. Payroll mechanics explain this sensitivity [24, 27]. ABM pays roughly 113,000 employees biweekly [2]. Meanwhile, enterprise clients take 45 to 65 days to settle invoices [24, 27]. A three-day slip in Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) traps roughly ~$70+ million in cash [24, 27].

web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: ABM is vastly healthier than Carillion—with $234.4M in FY2025 CFO and manageable 2.7x–2.9x net leverage—but Carillion is the base-rate warning for why low-margin (~1.9% net) facility roll-ups cannot afford fixed-price mispricing, runaway ERP billing delays, or unrestrained M&A debt [1, 24, 28].

web_blocks.title: Blind-Spot Audit: Unbilled Receivables Creep, Red-Zone Multiemployer Pensions & WOTC Expiration

web_blocks.html: Hidden Unit-Economics & Cash-Conversion Frictions: Three structural drags omitted from the baseline unit-economics view surfaced in FY2025–Q3 FY2026 filings. First, while 9M FY2026 operating cash flow rebounded to $275.0 million ($199.6 million FCF; full-year FCF guidance raised to ~$210 million), unbilled trade receivables rose 13.0% in nine months from $273.6 million to $309.1 million and costs incurred in excess of billings rose 8.3% to $209.8 million ($518.9 million combined vs. $1,193.7 million billed receivables, Q3 FY2026 10-Q Note 4). Unsatisfied remaining performance obligations stood at $287.3 million (77% over 12 months), reflecting lumpy RavenVolt/ATS project milestones. Second, per the FY2025 Form 10-K, roughly 45% of ABM's 113,000 employees (~51,000 workers) are covered by over 300 local collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) across more than 20 unions, with major CBA expirations clustered across 2026–2029. Multiemployer defined-benefit pension contributions climbed from $73.6 million (FY23) to $82.3 million (FY25)—including $23.7 million to Building Service 32BJ and $20.5 million to the Red-Zone (<65% funded) SEIU National Industry Pension Fund, which operates under a Rehabilitation Plan with statutory surcharges imposed. Third, per Q3 FY2026 10-Q Note 12, federal Work Opportunity Tax Credits (WOTC) and FEZ hiring credits expired on December 31, 2025 without renewal, eliminating tax offsets for 2026+ hires and lifting ABM's normalized effective tax rate to 29%–30% [42, 48].

book_paragraphs: To see how ABM Industries actually makes—and occasionally loses—money, follow a single dollar of revenue from the moment a client signs a contract to the moment cash lands in ABM's bank account.

First, how does ABM win that dollar? Not with viral marketing or a frictionless self-serve app, but through grueling, months-long Request for Proposal (RFP) battles. A Fortune 500 manufacturer, a municipal airport authority, or a school district puts its facility maintenance out to bid every three to five years. ABM's sales engineers walk the site, count square footage, audit union wage scales, and submit a multi-hundred-page proposal. Once inside the building, ABM plays the 'land and expand' game: start with janitorial, cross-sell stationary HVAC engineering, and layer on 'tag work'—those unscheduled repairs, special event cleanups, and emergency calls billed at premium hourly rates.

Now look at the audited FY2025 income waterfall—reconciled cleanly without double-counting amortization—because the numbers tell a sobering story about margin tolerance. ABM collected $8,745.9 million in revenue. Direct operating expenses (excluding $53.1 million of property and equipment depreciation, but embedding $4,917.9 million in direct labor, union benefits, supplies, and subcontractors) consumed $7,617.7 million, or 87.1 cents of every dollar. SG&A took $697.4 million, restructuring charges took $13.4 million, and total audited depreciation and amortization—$53.1 million of PP&E depreciation plus $52.5 million of acquisition intangible amortization, or $105.6 million combined—took the rest. That left exact GAAP operating profit of $311.7 million, a slim 3.56% margin.

Then came the lender's cut. Because ABM financed its M&A spree with debt, interest expense took $96.4 million—nearly 31% of entire GAAP operating profit. Offset modestly by $4.6 million in unconsolidated affiliate income and reduced by $57.6 million in income taxes, ABM kept $162.4 million in GAAP net income. That is a 1.86% net margin: on every $100 of services ABM delivers, less than $2 drops to the bottom line.

When a business runs on 1.9% net margins, two operational mechanics become existential: contract pricing discipline and working capital velocity. On pricing, ABM splits its book between cost-plus contracts (where union wage hikes pass straight to the customer) and fixed-price contracts (where ABM eats any unexpected labor inflation until the contract reopens). On working capital, ABM pays 113,000 workers every two weeks like clockwork, while waiting weeks or months for corporate clients to pay their invoices. During the peak of ABM's ELEVATE ERP software rollout, billing friction and unbilled receivables crushed operating cash flow to just $20.4 million in FY2022. By FY2025, cash flow had recovered to $234.4 million—still well below the $457.5 million peak seen in FY2020, but enough to generate $155.1 million in free cash flow after $79.3 million in capital expenditures.

Three additional unit-economic frictions also deserve close monitoring in 2026. Even as nine-month operating cash flow rebounded to $275.0 million, unbilled receivables and unbilled project costs climbed to $518.9 million combined, showing that project-heavy engineering work stretches billing cycles. Meanwhile, multiemployer pension contributions reached $82.3 million—including $20.5 million into the underfunded Red-Zone SEIU National Industry Pension Fund carrying statutory surcharges—ahead of a heavy 2026–2029 union contract renewal calendar. Finally, federal WOTC hiring tax credits expired on December 31, 2025 without Congressional renewal, creating a quiet normalized tax-rate headwind toward 29%–30%.

book_subsections.title: The Base-Rate Warning: Why Low-Margin Roll-Ups Break
paragraphs: History offers a sharp warning for low-margin facility operators. Between 2014 and 2018, UK-based Carillion plc grew into a massive facilities management and contracting giant through debt-funded acquisitions and fixed-price tenders. When contract costs crept up and working capital slowed down, Carillion's ~2%–3% margins offered zero shock absorber, ending in compulsory liquidation in 2018.

To be crystal clear, ABM is nowhere near Carillion's distress—ABM generates positive free cash flow, maintains ~2.7x–2.9x leverage, and has raised its dividend for 58 straight years. Yet the Carillion base rate explains why you and I must watch ABM's fixed-price contract discipline and ERP billing cycle like a hawk.

In a labor-intensive business with 113,000 employees on biweekly payroll, cash timing is just as important as accounting profit. Every day of billing delay inside an ERP transition ties up tens of millions of dollars in unbilled receivables. Once ABM's ELEVATE systems fully stabilize, freeing up just three to five days of working capital could open $70 million to $120 million in incremental cash flow—a massive lever for a company generating $155 million in annual free cash flow.

book_subsections.title: Tracing the $100 Waterfall in Plain English
paragraphs: Let's translate Chapter 3's reconciled $100 revenue-to-free-cash-flow waterfall into a mental picture you can carry into any earnings call, without double-counting depreciation. Out of every $100 that walks in ABM's front door from a hospital, airport, or office tower, $87.10 goes straight back out for direct operating costs excluding depreciation (field labor, union benefits, supplies, and subcontractors). Another $8.13 goes to SG&A and restructuring, and $1.21 covers combined PP&E depreciation and acquisition intangible amortization.

That leaves exactly $3.56 of GAAP operating profit per $100 of sales. From there, interest on acquisition debt takes $1.10, unconsolidated affiliates add $0.05, and income taxes take $0.66—landing GAAP net income at $1.86 per $100 of sales. After working-capital swings and $0.91 of CapEx, free cash flow finishes at just $1.77 per $100. In a business with margins that thin, a minor slip in unbilled receivables or fixed-price union wages can wipe out an entire year's free cash flow.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A 1.86% net margin means there is almost no margin for operational sloppiness. If union wages jump 5% on a fixed-price contract, or if an ERP glitch delays customer invoicing by five days, free cash flow feels it immediately. Next, let's step outside ABM's walls and compare its economics against the best operators in the facilities and specialty contracting industry.
